verdict.rationale: The Hebrew word-cluster around parental discipline is dense and pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible). The nouns 'rod' (shevet, H7626) and 'discipline' (musar, H4148) and the verb 'to discipline' (yasar, H3256) recur across Proverbs with parallel terms 'reproof' (tokachat, H8433) and 'wisdom' (chokmah, H2451). Proverbs 23:13-14 uses the verb 'to strike' (nakah, H5221) with 'rod' (shevet) plus the explicit clause that the child will not 'die' (mut, H4191), which is grammatically the most physical of the anchors. At the same time the same Solomonic cluster commands 'discipline' (yasar) without any 'rod' (shevet) in Proverbs 29:17 and Proverbs 19:18, so the canon supplies two parental discipline patterns that the words themselves do not rank. The New Testament brake terms 'provoke to anger' (paroggizo, G3949) in Ephesians 6:4 and 'provoke' (erethizo, G2042) with 'become discouraged' (athymeo, G0120) in Colossians 3:21 lexically forbid the provoking and discouraging mode. The Hebrews 12 vocabulary 'to train or discipline a child' (paideuo, G3811) and the severe term 'to scourge' (mastigoo, G3146, used six other times in the Gospels for literal flogging) frames divine teaching in striking imagery, and Revelation 3:19 ties 'warm love' (phileo, G5368) with 'rebuke' (elencho, G1651) and 'discipline' (paideuo). The lexical pattern decisively affirms parental discipline and decisively forbids the provoking mode, but underdetermines whether the corporal mode specifically is mandated, permitted, or pictured figuratively, so the verdict is materially contested rather than affirmed or denied.

scripture.force: Proverbs 13:24 pairs one who 'withholds' (chasak, H2820) his 'rod' (shevet, H7626) against one who 'loves' (ahav, H0157) his son and seeks him with 'discipline' (musar, H4148). The Hebrew poetic structure aligns the two clauses antithetically (as opposites), and the rod functions as a stock figure standing for corrective action. Whether 'rod' (shevet) here denotes a physical striking instrument or operates as a wisdom-genre figure for parental correction generally is the central contested lexical point, because the same noun elsewhere means shepherd staff, governing scepter, and tribal authority.

Proverbs 22:15 says 'folly' (ivvelet, H0200) is bound up in the heart of a 'youth' (naar, H5288), and the 'rod of discipline' (shevet musar, H7626 + H4148) drives it far from him. The genitive (a noun in the 'of-X' grammatical form) chaining of 'rod' (shevet) to 'discipline' (musar) in the Masoretic text (the standard Hebrew text tradition) reads the rod as the instrument or embodiment of discipline rather than as bare violence, which both supports a corporal reading and leaves room for 'rod' (shevet) as a figure for corrective authority paired with the discipline noun.

Proverbs 23:13 says: Do not 'withhold' (mana, the verbal sense) from a 'youth' (naar, H5288) 'discipline' (musar, H4148), for if you 'strike' (nakah, H5221) him with the 'rod' (shevet, H7626) he will not 'die' (mut, H4191). The verb 'to strike' (nakah) is the standard Hebrew verb for striking or smiting and is grammatically physical, paired here with 'rod' (shevet) by means of the preposition 'b' (with the rod). This is the most lexically explicit corporal anchor in the canon, and the very clause that asserts the action also builds a hard bound into the saying, the child will not die, which lexically excludes lethal or severe harm. This is the strongest single text for a literal-corporal reading and at the same time builds in a built-in lethality limit.

Proverbs 23:14 says: You shall 'strike' (nakah, H5221) him with the 'rod' (shevet, H7626) and 'deliver' (natsal, H5337) his 'soul' (nephesh) from Sheol (the realm of the dead). The continuation extends the 'strike with rod' (nakah plus shevet) collocation and frames the disciplinary aim soteriologically (in terms of salvation), as deliverance from Sheol rather than retribution. Lexically the verse foregrounds a saving, formation-oriented intent for the physical act, which neither softens the literal sense of 'to strike' (nakah) nor reduces the act to a metaphor on its own grammatical terms.

Proverbs 29:15 says the 'rod' (shevet, H7626) and 'reproof' (tokachat, H8433) give 'wisdom' (chokmah, H2451), but a 'youth' (naar, H5288) left to himself shames his mother. The explicit pairing of 'rod' (shevet) with verbal reproof signals that the disciplinary instrument operates alongside formative speech toward a wisdom aim, which complicates reading 'rod' (shevet) as purely physical force isolated from instructive speech.

Proverbs 29:17 says: 'Discipline' (yasar, H3256) your son and he will give you rest, he will give delights to your soul. The parental command here uses the verb 'to discipline' (yasar) without any mention of 'rod' (shevet), and the immediate aim is restful relationship and delight. This is lexically important because the same Solomonic cluster that elsewhere foregrounds the rod here commands discipline without the rod-image, showing that the disciplinary frame is broader than the corporal mode and does not depend on 'rod' (shevet) as the sole instrument.

Proverbs 19:18 says: 'Discipline' (yasar, H3256) your son while there is hope, but do not set your soul on his 'death' (mut, H4191). The proverb commands parental discipline using 'to discipline' (yasar) and explicitly forbids any orientation toward the child's death, which builds a severity bound directly into the lexical command. As with Proverbs 29:17 the parental imperative does not require 'rod' (shevet), and as with Proverbs 23:13 the saying installs a lethality limit on whatever disciplinary action is in view.

Deuteronomy 8:5 says: As a man 'disciplines' (yasar, H3256) his son, so the LORD your God 'disciplines' (yasar) you. The parental disciplinary act is presented as the analogical ground for divine teaching, which assumes parental discipline as a known and legitimate practice and treats 'to discipline' (yasar) as the descriptive verb. The verse is parental-discipline assuming, not method-prescribing, and does not specify corporal or non-corporal mode.

Hebrews 12:6 says: Whom the Lord 'loves' (agapao, G0025) he 'disciplines' (paideuo, G3811), and 'scourges' (mastigoo, G3146) every son he receives. The verb 'to train or discipline a child' (paideuo) carries the broad sense of child-rearing and correction, and the clause ties discipline to love rather than to wrath. The parallel verb 'to scourge' (mastigoo) is the standard term for literal scourging or flogging, used elsewhere in the Gospels for the physical scourging inflicted on Jesus, so the divine teaching image in this verse is lexically severe even though it is framed as love. The verse establishes the loving qualifier of the proposition but speaks to divine discipline by analogy to parental discipline, which makes its bearing on the parental method by inference rather than by direct command.

Hebrews 12:11 says: No 'discipline' (paideia, G3809) seems joyful at the time but grievous, yet afterward it yields the 'peaceable' (eirenikos, G1516) fruit of 'righteousness' (dikaiosune, G1343) to those 'trained' (gumnazo, G1128, used as athletic training) by it. The stated end-goal is peaceable righteousness, which lexically bounds legitimate discipline toward a restorative outcome and stands against any abusive or wrathful practice, while the participle 'to train' (gumnazo) casts the disciplined as athletes-in-training, framing the experience as formative rather than punitive.

Ephesians 6:4 says: Fathers, do not 'provoke to anger' (paroggizo, G3949) your children but bring them up in the 'discipline' (paideia, G3809) and 'admonition or instruction' (nouthesia, G3559) of the Lord. The negated imperative caps parental discipline with a prohibition against provoking, and pairs 'discipline' (paideia) with the verbal-formation term 'admonition' (nouthesia), which lexically supports the proposition that abusive or exasperating practice is excluded while measured formation is commanded. The verse forbids the harsh mode but does not specify or prohibit the corporal mode by name.

Colossians 3:21 says: Fathers, do not 'provoke' (erethizo, G2042) your children, lest they 'become discouraged' (athymeo, G0120). The pair 'provoke' (erethizo) plus 'become discouraged' (athymeo) gives a second, independent New Testament prohibition against the provoking mode of parenting and adds a psychological outcome bound, the loss of heart, which is grammatically distinct from Ephesians 6:4 yet pointed in the same direction. Lexically this strengthens the canon-wide brake on harshness without addressing the corporal mode itself.

Revelation 3:19 says: Those whom I 'love' (phileo, G5368) I 'rebuke' (elencho, G1651) and 'discipline' (paideuo, G3811). The chain 'love' (phileo) plus 'rebuke' (elencho) plus 'discipline' (paideuo) lexically binds warm affection to verbal reproof and to disciplinary action, which rebuts any reading in which divine love precludes correction. The verse uses 'warm love' (phileo) rather than 'committed love' (agapao), distinguishing the bond as familial-affectionate, and frames discipline as an expression of that love.

complicating_texts.resolution: The same Solomonic discipline cluster commands the parent to 'discipline' (yasar, H3256) the son with no 'rod' (shevet, H7626) in view, and frames the aim as restful relationship and delight to the soul. This shows that the canon supplies a 'discipline-without-rod' (yasar-without-shevet) parental imperative inside the very corpus where the rod texts sit, so the disciplinary frame is broader than the corporal mode and does not lexically require the rod as the indispensable instrument. The complication is addressed by recognizing that 'rod' (shevet) is one figure within a broader 'discipline and instruction' (yasar and musar) frame, not the sole prescribed instrument.

The verse commands 'discipline' (yasar, H3256) and explicitly forbids any orientation toward the child's 'death' (mut, H4191), which builds a severity bound directly into the lexical command. This harmonizes with the non-abusive qualifier of the proposition and with Proverbs 23:13's 'he-will-not-die' clause, the rod-cluster texts themselves contain internal limits on severity. The complication is addressed by reading the proverbs together as a self-bounding discipline-frame.

The prohibition against 'provoking to anger' (paroggizo, G3949) children sits in the same clause as the command to 'discipline' (paideia, G3809), so the verse simultaneously authorizes formative discipline and forbids the harsh or abusive form. This is consistent with the measured, non-abusive qualifier of the proposition and does not contradict it.

The pair 'provoke' (erethizo, G2042) plus 'become discouraged' (athymeo, G0120) gives a second, independent New Testament prohibition against the provoking mode of parenting, lexically distinct from 'provoke to anger' (paroggizo) in Ephesians 6:4. The complication is addressed by treating the two prohibitions as a canon-wide brake on harshness, which the proposition's measured-and-not-abusive qualifier honors.

The stated end of discipline is the 'peaceable' (eirenikos, G1516) fruit of 'righteousness' (dikaiosune, G1343), which bounds legitimate discipline away from wrath and toward restorative outcome. It complicates a maximal reading of the rod texts but harmonizes with the loving and measured framing of the proposition.

The verb 'to scourge' (mastigoo, G3146) used here for divine discipline is the standard Greek term for literal scourging, used six other times in the Gospels for the physical flogging of Christ. This complicates any reading that takes the New Testament vocabulary as softening the corporal image of OT discipline, because the divine-teaching analogy in Hebrews 12 itself uses a grammatically severe term. The complication is addressed by noting that the verse is divine-analogical rather than parental-prescriptive, and that the surrounding clauses cap severity through 'to discipline' (paideuo) and the peaceable-fruit end-goal.

The word 'rod' (shevet, H7626) carries multiple meanings across literal rod, shepherd staff, and governing scepter, and the wisdom-genre saying compresses both prescription and figure into a single line. The lexical store alone cannot determine, for this verse on its own grammatical terms, whether the proverb prescribes physical striking as the operative mode or commands corrective parental authority figured under the rod-image. Proverbs 23:13-14 makes the physical reading explicit through 'to strike' (nakah), but Proverbs 13:24 by itself remains underdetermined on the corporal-specific point and is the locus of the contemporary lexical dispute.

variants.note: No variant units supplied in the bundle and the cited books fall outside ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) scope. The Hebrew Proverbs anchors are textually stable for the disciplinary terms across Masoretic witnesses (the standard Hebrew text tradition), and the New Testament readings of 'discipline' (paideia), 'provoke to anger' (paroggizo), 'provoke' (erethizo), 'to scourge' (mastigoo), and the 'love-rebuke-discipline' (phileo-elencho-paideuo) chain in Revelation 3:19 are not in dispute among the cited witnesses.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads Proverbs 23:13-14 at face value, the verb 'to strike' (nakah, H5221) plus 'rod' (shevet, H7626) is grammatically physical, and the very clause that commands the act installs a lethality bound, he will not die. The same cluster (Proverbs 13:24, 22:15, 29:15) treats the rod as a real disciplinary instrument paired with 'discipline' (musar) and 'reproof' (tokachat), and the New Testament does not retract the parental imperative but only forbids the harsh, provoking mode. On this lens the proposition's loving-measured-and-not-abusive corporal practice is directly affirmed.

Treats Proverbs as wisdom-genre generalizations that use 'rod' (shevet) as a figure for corrective parental authority within the broader frame of 'discipline' (yasar) and 'instruction' (musar). Proverbs 29:17 and Proverbs 19:18 command parental discipline without any 'rod' (shevet), showing that the figure is not the indispensable instrument but one image within the discipline-frame. On this lens the proverbs commend disciplined formation without binding parents to a specific corporal method, leaving the corporal-specific claim underdetermined.

Foregrounds Ephesians 6:4 ('provoke to anger' (paroggizo) prohibition), Colossians 3:21 ('provoke' (erethizo) plus 'become discouraged' (athymeo) prohibition), and Hebrews 12:11 (peaceable-fruit end-goal with 'to train' (gumnazo) athletic training imagery), where discipline is bounded against provocation and aimed at peaceable righteousness. On this lens abusive practice is clearly excluded while the permissibility of the corporal mode itself is left to application rather than mandated lexically. The Hebrews 12:6 'to scourge' (mastigoo) image is read as analogical-divine, not as a parental method-prescription.

Reads Proverbs 23:13-14 literally ('strike with rod' (nakah plus shevet) is grammatically explicit physical striking) but treats the proverbs as a self-bounding cluster, the rod text itself installs the lethality limit (he will not die) and pairs with verbal 'reproof' (tokachat, H8433) and instructive 'discipline' (yasar, H3256). The New Testament brakes ('provoke to anger' (paroggizo), 'provoke' (erethizo), peaceable-fruit end-goal) are read as compatible severity-caps on a permitted but limited corporal mode rather than as redirecting the mode itself. On this lens the proposition's loving-measured-and-not-abusive practice is affirmed and the cultural-and-legal qualifier becomes the prudential outworking.

Traces the discipline-frame across 'to discipline' (yasar, H3256) and 'discipline' (musar, H4148) in the OT and 'discipline' (paideia, G3809) and 'to train or discipline a child' (paideuo, G3811) in the NT, finds the throughline to be formation toward wisdom and righteousness rather than any specific method, and observes that the canon supplies both rod-cluster texts and yasar-without-rod texts inside the same Solomonic corpus. On this lens the lexical pattern decisively affirms the disciplinary aim and the severity-cap, but the method question is treated as a wisdom-application matter that the words underdetermine, hence disputed.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on whether the Hebrew wisdom proverbs are read as method-specific prescription or as genre-typical commendation of corrective discipline figured under the rod, whether Proverbs 23:13-14's 'strike-with-rod' (nakah-plus-shevet) is the canonical anchor for a literal corporal mode or a particularly vivid figure inside a broader 'discipline' (yasar) frame, and how the New Testament discipline vocabulary bounds severity. Analogia scripturae (the principle of interpreting Scripture by Scripture) harmonizes the rod texts with the Ephesians 6:4 and Colossians 3:21 brakes and with the peaceable-fruit end-goal in Hebrews 12:11.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What do the disciplinary terms in the cited texts, the Hebrew 'rod' (shevet), 'discipline' (musar), 'to discipline' (yasar), and 'to strike' (nakah) in Proverbs and Deuteronomy, and the Greek 'discipline' (paideia), 'to train or discipline a child' (paideuo), 'to scourge' (mastigoo), 'provoke to anger' (paroggizo), and 'provoke' (erethizo) in the New Testament, indicate about whether and how Scripture treats physical correction of young children, including any bounds it places on severity and any cultural or legal qualifications it installs by its own grammar.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem embeds three evaluative qualifiers, that corporal discipline is permitted, that loving and measured forms are in view, and that abusive practice is sinful and unlawful, and a fourth contextual qualifier about cultural and legal application, which together preload a permissive-with-limits verdict. The lexicon strongly supports the severity-cap qualifier via 'provoke to anger' (paroggizo) in Ephesians 6:4, 'provoke' (erethizo) plus 'become discouraged' (athymeo) in Colossians 3:21, the peaceable-fruit end-goal in Hebrews 12:11, and the internal Proverbs limits in Proverbs 23:13 (he will not die) and Proverbs 19:18 (do not set your soul on his death). The lexicon also supplies a grammatically explicit corporal anchor in Proverbs 23:13-14 through 'strike-with-rod' (nakah plus shevet). The permissibility of the corporal mode specifically rests on whether the Proverbs 23 anchor is read as universal binding prescription, as bounded permission, or as a vivid wisdom-figure within a broader 'discipline' (yasar) frame that the canon elsewhere commands without the rod. The verdict is derived on the original stem and reported as disputed because the lexicon decisively affirms the disciplinary aim and the severity-cap but underdetermines the method question.

lay_summary: The Hebrew Proverbs cluster around parental discipline uses several closely linked words. 'Rod' (shevet) appears with 'discipline' (musar) in Proverbs 13:24, 22:15, and 29:15. Proverbs 23:13-14 goes further, using the verb 'to strike' (nakah) with 'rod' (shevet) and adding the clause he will not die, so the corporal image is grammatically as explicit as the Hebrew gets and at the same time installs its own lethality bound. The same Solomonic cluster then turns around and commands the parent to 'discipline' (yasar) the son in Proverbs 29:17 and Proverbs 19:18 without any mention of the rod, and Proverbs 19:18 again forbids any orientation toward the child's death. So the canon supplies both a rod-pattern and a discipline-without-rod pattern inside the same body of wisdom sayings. Deuteronomy 8:5 uses 'to discipline' (yasar) to describe parental discipline as the analogical ground for divine discipline. In the New Testament the parental command in Ephesians 6:4 places 'training' (paideia) alongside an explicit prohibition, do not 'provoke to anger' (paroggizo) your children. Colossians 3:21 repeats the brake with different words, do not 'provoke' (erethizo) lest they 'become discouraged' (athymeo). Hebrews 12 frames divine discipline as the work of a loving Father, uses 'to discipline' (paideuo) and even the severe term 'to scourge' (mastigoo, the same verb used for the literal scourging of Christ), and lands the discussion on the peaceable fruit of righteousness in those trained by it. Revelation 3:19 ties 'warm love' (phileo) to 'rebuke' (elencho) and 'discipline' (paideuo). Reading the canon together, the words clearly affirm two things, that parental discipline is commanded as an expression of love and that the harsh, provoking, exasperating mode is forbidden. What the words do not settle on their own is whether the corporal mode specifically is mandated for every parent, permitted as one bounded method, or pictured under the rod-figure as one image within a broader discipline-frame, because 'rod' (shevet) is a flexible noun, Proverbs 29:17 commands discipline without it, and the New Testament brakes do not address the corporal mode by name. That is why the lexical evidence is best described as genuinely contested.
